items.rec: Publish a vulnerability disclosure policy with a monitored security contact address, and define an internal triage and response SLA for inbound reports. (CSF ID.RA-08: Processes for receiving, analyzing, and responding to vulnerability di…)

items.q: Perform Automated Operating System Patch Management — Perform operating system updates on enterprise assets through automated patch management on a monthly, or more frequent, basis.
items.rec: Maintain automated operating system patch management with monthly or more frequent deployment, and report compliance against the documented SLA.

items.q: Perform Automated Application Patch Management — Perform application updates on enterprise assets through automated patch management on a monthly, or more frequent, basis.
items.rec: Bring third-party application patching under automated management so it meets the same SLA as operating system patching, and remediate the current backlog of out-of-date applications.

items.q: Perform Automated Vulnerability Scans of Internal Enterprise Assets — Perform automated vulnerability scans of internal enterprise assets on a quarterly, or more frequent, basis. Conduct both authenticated and unauthenticated scans.
items.rec: Maintain authenticated automated vulnerability scanning of internal enterprise assets on at least a monthly cadence, covering servers and endpoints.

items.q: Perform Automated Vulnerability Scans of Externally-Exposed Enterprise Assets — Perform automated vulnerability scans of externally-exposed enterprise assets. Perform scans on a monthly, or more frequent, basis.
items.rec: Maintain automated vulnerability scanning of externally exposed assets on at least a monthly cadence, with results reviewed on a fixed schedule.

items.q: Remediate Detected Vulnerabilities — Remediate detected vulnerabilities in software through processes and tooling on a monthly, or more frequent, basis, based on the remediation process.
items.rec: Remediate detected vulnerabilities within the documented SLA by severity, and report median time to close as a performance measure.

items.q: Collect Audit Logs — Collect audit logs. Ensure that logging, per the enterprise’s audit log management process, has been enabled across enterprise assets.
items.rec: Increase log retention for firewall, hypervisor and network sources to meet the documented retention standard, provisioning storage or a central log platform as required. (CSF PR.PS-04: Log records are generated and made available for continuous monitoring)

items.q: Ensure Adequate Audit Log Storage — Ensure that logging destinations maintain adequate storage to comply with the enterprise’s audit log management process.
items.rec: Provision sufficient audit log storage to support the documented retention period across all in-scope sources, and alert on approaching storage exhaustion.

items.q: Retain Audit Logs — Retain audit logs across enterprise assets for a minimum of 90 days.
items.rec: Meet the documented log retention standard across all sources, provisioning additional storage or a central log platform for the sources currently falling short.

items.q: Standardize Time Synchronization — Standardize time synchronization. Configure at least two synchronized time sources across enterprise assets, where supported.
items.rec: Maintain centralised time synchronisation from at least two authoritative sources across all assets, so that log timestamps are reliable for correlation.

items.q: Collect Detailed Audit Logs — Configure detailed audit logging for enterprise assets containing sensitive data. Include event source, date, username, timestamp, source addresses, destination addresses, and other useful elements that could assist in a forensic investigation.
items.rec: Enable detailed audit logging beyond the platform default, including process creation with command line, script block logging and authentication detail.

items.q: Collect DNS Query Audit Logs — Collect DNS query audit logs on enterprise assets, where appropriate and supported.
items.rec: Collect DNS query audit logs, retain them in line with the retention standard, and make them available for investigation and detection use cases.

items.q: Collect URL Request Audit Logs — Collect URL request audit logs on enterprise assets, where appropriate and supported.
items.rec: Collect URL request audit logs from the web filtering platform and retain them in line with the documented retention standard.

items.q: Collect Command-Line Audit Logs — Collect command-line audit logs. Example implementations include collecting audit logs from PowerShell®, BASH™, and remote administrative terminals.
items.rec: Enable command-line process auditing across servers and endpoints and forward the events centrally. Absence of this data materially extends investigation time and should be treated as a priority.

items.q: Centralize Audit Logs — Centralize, to the extent possible, audit log collection and retention across enterprise assets in accordance with the documented audit log management process. Example implementations primarily include leveraging a SIEM tool to centralize multiple log sources.
items.rec: Deploy a central log aggregation capability covering identity, endpoint, network, hypervisor and cloud sources. This is the foundational gap behind most detection and investigation findings and should be sequenced first.

items.q: Conduct Audit Log Reviews — Conduct reviews of audit logs to detect anomalies or abnormal events that could indicate a potential threat. Conduct reviews on a weekly, or more frequent, basis.
items.rec: Develop analysis playbooks for the most likely event types so that quality of analysis does not depend on who is available, and record analysis outcomes in a consistent form. (CSF DE.AE-02: Potentially adverse events are analyzed to better understand associate…)

items.q: Collect Service Provider Logs — Collect service provider logs, where supported. Example implementations include collecting authentication and authorization events, data creation and disposal events, and user management events.
items.rec: Collect service provider and cloud platform logs into the central log store so that third-party administrative activity is visible and reviewable.

items.q: Ensure Use of Only Fully Supported Browsers and Email Clients — Ensure only fully supported browsers and email clients are allowed to execute in the enterprise, only using the latest version of browsers and email clients provided through the vendor.
items.rec: Maintain only fully supported browsers and email clients, kept current through automated update management.

items.q: Use DNS Filtering Services — Use DNS filtering services on all end-user devices, including remote and on-premises assets, to block access to known malicious domains.
items.rec: Maintain DNS filtering services on all enterprise assets including remote workers, with bypass prevented at the network perimeter.

items.q: Maintain and Enforce Network-Based URL Filters — Enforce and update network-based URL filters to limit an enterprise asset from connecting to potentially malicious or unapproved websites. Example implementations include category-based filtering, reputation-based filtering, or through the use of block lists. Enforce filters for all enterprise assets.
items.rec: Maintain and enforce network-based URL filtering with category-based blocking, applied consistently on-network and over the VPN.

items.q: Restrict Unnecessary or Unauthorized Browser and Email Client Extensions — Restrict, either through uninstalling or disabling, any unauthorized or unnecessary browser or email client plugins, extensions, and add-on applications.
items.rec: Restrict unauthorised browser and email client extensions through managed policy, permitting only an approved extension list.

items.q: Implement DMARC — To lower the chance of spoofed or modified emails from valid domains, implement DMARC policy and verification, starting with implementing the Sender Policy Framework (SPF) and the DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) standards.
items.rec: Complete the DMARC deployment by moving the policy to p=reject once report analysis confirms no legitimate sending sources remain unauthenticated.

items.q: Block Unnecessary File Types — Block unnecessary file types attempting to enter the enterprise’s email gateway.
items.rec: Maintain blocking of unnecessary and high-risk file types at the email gateway, and review the blocked type list periodically.

items.q: Deploy and Maintain Email Server Anti-Malware Protections — Deploy and maintain email server anti-malware protections, such as attachment scanning and/or sandboxing.
items.rec: Maintain email server anti-malware protections including attachment detonation and link rewriting across the tenant.

items.q: Deploy and Maintain Anti-Malware Software — Deploy and maintain anti-malware software on all enterprise assets.
items.rec: Extend endpoint and server detection coverage to 100% of managed assets and establish an out-of-hours triage capability, whether in-house rota or a managed detection service, with a measured acknowledgement target. (CSF DE.CM-09: Computing hardware and software, runtime environments, and their data …)

items.q: Configure Automatic Anti-Malware Signature Updates — Configure automatic updates for anti-malware signature files on all enterprise assets.
items.rec: Maintain automatic anti-malware signature and engine updates, with console reporting confirming currency across the estate.

items.q: Disable Autorun and Autoplay for Removable Media — Disable autorun and autoplay auto-execute functionality for removable media.
items.rec: Maintain autorun and autoplay disablement for removable media across all enterprise assets through managed policy.

items.q: Configure Automatic Anti-Malware Scanning of Removable Media — Configure anti-malware software to automatically scan removable media.
items.rec: Maintain automatic anti-malware scanning of removable media on connection across all endpoints.

items.q: Enable Anti-Exploitation Features — Enable anti-exploitation features on enterprise assets and software, where possible, such as Microsoft® Data Execution Prevention (DEP), Windows® Defender Exploit Guard (WDEG), or Apple® System Integrity Protection (SIP) and Gatekeeper™.
items.rec: Complete deployment of anti-exploitation features, including moving the remaining recommended attack surface reduction rules from audit into block mode following a monitoring period.

items.q: Centrally Manage Anti-Malware Software — Centrally manage anti-malware software.
items.rec: Maintain centrally managed anti-malware software with alerting, and close the remaining endpoint coverage gap to reach full deployment.

items.q: Use Behavior-Based Anti-Malware Software — Use behavior-based anti-malware software.
items.rec: Assign named ownership for reviewing identity risk and user activity alerts, with a defined review cadence and evidence of triage, so that generated alerts are actually acted upon. (CSF DE.CM-03: Personnel activity and technology usage are monitored to find potentia…)

items.q: Establish and Maintain a Data Recovery Process — Establish and maintain a documented data recovery process that includes detailed backup procedures. In the process, address the scope of data recovery activities, recovery prioritization, and the security of backup data. Review and update documentation annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard.
items.rec: Maintain the documented data recovery process covering scope, schedule, retention and testing, and reinstate the documented restore-testing cadence.

items.q: Perform Automated Backups — Perform automated backups of in-scope enterprise assets. Run backups weekly, or more frequently, based on the sensitivity of the data.
items.rec: Maintain backups to the documented 3-2-1 standard with immutability, and restore the full restore-testing cycle including at least one full system recovery test per year rather than file-level tests only. (CSF PR.DS-11: Backups of data are created, protected, maintained, and tested)

items.q: Protect Recovery Data — Protect recovery data with equivalent controls to the original data. Reference encryption or data separation, based on requirements.
items.rec: Maintain backups to the documented 3-2-1 standard with immutability, and restore the full restore-testing cycle including at least one full system recovery test per year rather than file-level tests only. (CSF PR.DS-11: Backups of data are created, protected, maintained, and tested)

items.q: Establish and Maintain an Isolated Instance of Recovery Data — Establish and maintain an isolated instance of recovery data. Example implementations include, version controlling backup destinations through offline, cloud, or off-site systems or services.
items.rec: Maintain an isolated, immutable instance of recovery data and verify immutability and offsite copy integrity on a defined cycle.

items.q: Test Data Recovery — Test backup recovery quarterly, or more frequently, for a sampling of in-scope enterprise assets.
items.rec: Maintain backups to the documented 3-2-1 standard with immutability, and restore the full restore-testing cycle including at least one full system recovery test per year rather than file-level tests only. (CSF PR.DS-11: Backups of data are created, protected, maintained, and tested)

items.q: Ensure Network Infrastructure is Up-to-Date — Ensure network infrastructure is kept up-to-date. Example implementations include running the latest stable release of software and/or using currently supported network as a service (NaaS) offerings. Review software versions monthly, or more frequently, to verify software support.
items.rec: Keep network infrastructure current and replace devices that are past vendor end-of-support and can no longer receive security updates.

items.q: Establish and Maintain a Secure Network Architecture — Design and maintain a secure network architecture. A secure network architecture must address segmentation, least privilege, and availability, at a minimum. Example implementations may include documentation, policy, and design components.
items.rec: Reduce east-west exposure within the corporate network through internal segmentation or host-based firewall policy, so that flat-network lateral movement is constrained. (CSF PR.IR-01: Networks and environments are protected from unauthorized logical acce…)

items.q: Securely Manage Network Infrastructure — Securely manage network infrastructure. Example implementations include version-controlled Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC), and the use of secure network protocols, such as SSH and HTTPS.
items.rec: Manage all network infrastructure securely from a dedicated management network using individual accounts and encrypted protocols, removing remaining plaintext management access.

items.q: Establish and Maintain Architecture Diagram(s) — Establish and maintain architecture diagram(s) and/or other network system documentation. Review and update documentation annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard.
items.rec: Establish and maintain architecture diagrams for all sites, and make diagram updates a mandatory deliverable of the change and integration process.

items.q: Centralize Network Authentication, Authorization, and Auditing (AAA) — Centralize network AAA.
items.rec: Centralise network authentication, authorisation and accounting so that network device access is managed from the central directory rather than local accounts.

items.q: Use of Secure Network Management and Communication Protocols — Adopt secure network management protocols (e.g., 802.1X) and secure communication protocols (e.g., Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 (WPA2) Enterprise or more secure alternatives).
items.rec: Use secure network management and communication protocols throughout, replacing legacy protocols such as SNMPv2c with authenticated, encrypted equivalents.

items.q: Ensure Remote Devices Utilize a VPN and are Connecting to an Enterprise’s AAA Infrastructure — Require users to authenticate to enterprise-managed VPN and authentication services prior to accessing enterprise resources on end-user devices.
items.rec: Require remote devices to connect through a VPN to enterprise-managed infrastructure, with split tunnelling disabled and device compliance enforced.

items.q: Establish and Maintain Dedicated Computing Resources for All Administrative Work — Establish and maintain dedicated computing resources, either physically or logically separated, for all administrative tasks or tasks requiring administrative access. The computing resources should be segmented from the enterprise's primary network and not be allowed internet access.
items.rec: Establish dedicated privileged access workstations for administrative work, isolated from email and general internet browsing.

items.q: Deploy a Host-Based Intrusion Detection Solution — Deploy a host-based intrusion detection solution on enterprise assets, where appropriate and/or supported.
items.rec: Maintain host-based intrusion detection across servers and endpoints, closing any remaining deployment gaps.

items.q: Deploy a Network Intrusion Detection Solution — Deploy a network intrusion detection solution on enterprise assets, where appropriate. Example implementations include the use of a Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS) or equivalent cloud service provider (CSP) service.
items.rec: Extend intrusion detection beyond the perimeter to internal network segments, so lateral movement is visible as well as inbound attack traffic.

items.q: Perform Traffic Filtering Between Network Segments — Perform traffic filtering between network segments, where appropriate.
items.rec: Maintain traffic filtering between network segments and introduce filtering within the corporate segment to constrain lateral movement.

items.q: Manage Access Control for Remote Assets — Manage access control for assets remotely connecting to enterprise resources. Determine amount of access to enterprise resources based on: up-to-date anti-malware software installed, configuration compliance with the enterprise’s secure configuration process, and ensuring the operating system and applications are up-to-date.
items.rec: Maintain access control for remote assets, requiring device compliance verification before network or cloud access is granted.

items.q: Collect Network Traffic Flow Logs — Collect network traffic flow logs and/or network traffic to review and alert upon from network devices.
items.rec: Collect network traffic flow logs and retain them for investigation and detection use, providing the network visibility currently absent.

items.q: Perform Application Layer Filtering — Perform application layer filtering. Example implementations include a filtering proxy, application layer firewall, or gateway.
items.rec: Define specific network monitoring use cases and thresholds, collect network flow data, and establish a baseline of normal traffic so that adverse events can be distinguished from routine activity. (CSF DE.CM-01: Networks and network services are monitored to find potentially advers…)

items.q: Deploy a Host-Based Intrusion Prevention Solution — Deploy a host-based intrusion prevention solution on enterprise assets, where appropriate and/or supported. Example implementations include use of an Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) client or host-based IPS agent.
items.rec: Maintain host-based intrusion prevention in blocking mode across servers and endpoints.

items.q: Deploy a Network Intrusion Prevention Solution — Deploy a network intrusion prevention solution, where appropriate. Example implementations include the use of a Network Intrusion Prevention System (NIPS) or equivalent CSP service.
items.rec: Extend intrusion prevention to internal network segments in addition to the perimeter.

items.q: Deploy Port-Level Access Control — Deploy port-level access control. Port-level access control utilizes 802.1x, or similar network access control protocols, such as certificates, and may incorporate user and/or device authentication.
items.rec: Deploy port-level access control such as 802.1X so that unauthorised devices connecting to physical network ports cannot reach the corporate network.

items.q: Tune Security Event Alerting Thresholds — Tune security event alerting thresholds monthly, or more frequently.
items.rec: Tune security event alerting thresholds away from vendor defaults on a defined review cycle, to reduce alert fatigue and improve signal quality.

items.q: Establish and Maintain a Security Awareness Program — Establish and maintain a security awareness program. The purpose of a security awareness program is to educate the enterprise’s workforce on how to interact with enterprise assets and data in a secure manner. Conduct training at hire and, at a minimum, annually. Review and update content annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard.
items.rec: Formalise leadership accountability for cybersecurity risk with a named executive owner, documented terms of reference, and a standing agenda item at the appropriate governance forum. Evidence leadership setting direction rather than only approving spend. (CSF GV.RR-01: Organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecu…)

items.q: Train Workforce Members to Recognize Social Engineering Attacks — Train workforce members to recognize social engineering attacks, such as phishing, business email compromise (BEC), pretexting, and tailgating.
items.rec: Maintain training on recognising social engineering attacks, reinforced by regular simulation, and trend the results over time.

items.q: Train Workforce Members on Authentication Best Practices — Train workforce members on authentication best practices. Example topics include MFA, password composition, and credential management.
items.rec: Maintain training on authentication best practice, including multi-factor authentication use and credential hygiene.

items.q: Train Workforce on Data Handling Best Practices — Train workforce members on how to identify and properly store, transfer, archive, and destroy sensitive data. This also includes training workforce members on clear screen and desk best practices, such as locking their screen when they step away from their enterprise asset, erasing physical and virtual whiteboards at the end of meetings, and storing data and assets securely.
items.rec: Deliver data handling training tied to the organisation's own classification scheme, so guidance is specific rather than generic.

items.q: Train Workforce Members on Causes of Unintentional Data Exposure — Train workforce members to be aware of causes for unintentional data exposure. Example topics include mis-delivery of sensitive data, losing a portable end-user device, or publishing data to unintended audiences.
items.rec: Maintain training on the causes of unintentional data exposure, including misdirected email and misconfigured sharing.

items.q: Train Workforce Members on Recognizing and Reporting Security Incidents — Train workforce members to be able to recognize a potential incident and be able to report such an incident.
items.rec: Maintain training and tooling for recognising and reporting security incidents, and provide feedback to reporters so reporting behaviour is reinforced.

items.q: Train Workforce on How to Identify and Report if Their Enterprise Assets are Missing Security Updates — Train workforce to understand how to verify and report out-of-date software patches or any failures in automated processes and tools. Part of this training should include notifying IT personnel of any failures in automated processes and tools.
items.rec: Train workforce members to identify and report out-of-date enterprise assets, and provide a simple self-service way for users to check device compliance status.

items.q: Train Workforce on the Dangers of Connecting to and Transmitting Enterprise Data Over Insecure Networks — Train workforce members on the dangers of connecting to, and transmitting data over, insecure networks for enterprise activities. If the enterprise has remote workers, training must include guidance to ensure that all users securely configure their home network infrastructure.
items.rec: Maintain training on the risks of insecure networks, supported technically by always-on VPN enforcement.

items.q: Conduct Role-Specific Security Awareness and Skills Training — Conduct role-specific security awareness and skills training. Example implementations include secure system administration courses for IT professionals, OWASP® Top 10 vulnerability awareness and prevention training for web application developers, and advanced social engineering awareness training for high-profile roles.
items.rec: Produce a cybersecurity RACI covering the main security activities, publish it beyond the IT function, and confirm through spot checks that staff outside IT know who owns security decisions. (CSF GV.RR-02: Roles, responsibilities, and authorities related to cybersecurity risk…)

items.q: Establish and Maintain an Inventory of Service Providers — Establish and maintain an inventory of service providers. The inventory is to list all known service providers, include classification(s), and designate an enterprise contact for each service provider. Review and update the inventory annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard.
items.rec: Extend the supplier list beyond spend-based tiering to identify which suppliers hold data, access systems or support critical services, and prioritise them by criticality rather than contract value. (CSF GV.SC-04: Suppliers are known and prioritized by criticality)

items.q: Establish and Maintain a Service Provider Management Policy — Establish and maintain a service provider management policy. Ensure the policy addresses the classification, inventory, assessment, monitoring, and decommissioning of service providers. Review and update the policy annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard.
items.rec: Establish a cybersecurity supply chain risk management programme with a documented strategy, policy, objectives and a named owner, agreed by the stakeholders responsible for procurement decisions. This underpins every other supply chain outcome and should be sequenced first. (CSF GV.SC-01: A cybersecurity supply chain risk management program, strategy, object…)

items.q: Classify Service Providers — Classify service providers. Classification consideration may include one or more characteristics, such as data sensitivity, data volume, availability requirements, applicable regulations, inherent risk, and mitigated risk. Update and review classifications annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard.
items.rec: Extend the supplier list beyond spend-based tiering to identify which suppliers hold data, access systems or support critical services, and prioritise them by criticality rather than contract value. (CSF GV.SC-04: Suppliers are known and prioritized by criticality)

items.q: Ensure Service Provider Contracts Include Security Requirements — Ensure service provider contracts include security requirements. Example requirements may include minimum security program requirements, security incident and/or data breach notification and response, data encryption requirements, and data disposal commitments. These security requirements must be consistent with the enterprise’s service provider management policy. Review service provider contracts annually to ensure contracts are not missing security requirements.
items.rec: Define standard cybersecurity roles and responsibilities for suppliers, customers and partners, and incorporate them into a reusable contractual security schedule applied to all new and renewing agreements. (CSF GV.SC-02: Cybersecurity roles and responsibilities for suppliers, customers, and…)

items.q: Assess Service Providers — Assess service providers consistent with the enterprise’s service provider management policy. Assessment scope may vary based on classification(s), and may include review of standardized assessment reports, such as Service Organization Control 2 (SOC 2) and Payment Card Industry (PCI) Attestation of Compliance (AoC), customized questionnaires, or other appropriately rigorous processes. Reassess service providers annually, at a minimum, or with new and renewed contracts.
items.rec: Introduce a mandatory pre-onboarding due diligence step for suppliers, proportionate to criticality, evidenced by an assurance artefact such as a current SOC 2, ISO 27001 certificate or completed questionnaire. (CSF GV.SC-06: Planning and due diligence are performed to reduce risks before enteri…)

items.q: Monitor Service Providers — Monitor service providers consistent with the enterprise’s service provider management policy. Monitoring may include periodic reassessment of service provider compliance, monitoring service provider release notes, and dark web monitoring.
items.rec: Assess, record and monitor the risk posed by suppliers and their products throughout the relationship, including periodic reassessment of critical suppliers and monitoring of supplier security notices and incidents. (CSF GV.SC-07: The risks posed by a supplier, their products and services, and other …)

items.q: Securely Decommission Service Providers — Securely decommission service providers. Example considerations include user and service account deactivation, termination of data flows, and secure disposal of enterprise data within service provider systems.
items.rec: Define supplier offboarding provisions covering data return or destruction, account termination and access revocation, and apply them within a defined period of contract end. (CSF GV.SC-10: Cybersecurity supply chain risk management plans include provisions fo…)

items.q: Apply Secure Design Principles in Application Architectures — Apply secure design principles in application architectures. Secure design principles include the concept of least privilege and enforcing mediation to validate every operation that the user makes, promoting the concept of "never trust user input." Examples include ensuring that explicit error checking is performed and documented for all input, including for size, data type, and acceptable ranges or formats. Secure design also means minimizing the application infrastructure attack surface, such as turning off unprotected ports and services, removing unnecessary programs and files, and renaming or removing default accounts.
items.rec: Extend secure development requirements to low-code and citizen development activity, introducing review, environment separation and a documented approval step for business-built applications and automations. (CSF PR.PS-06: Secure software development practices are integrated, and their perfor…)

items.q: Establish and Maintain a Process to Accept and Address Software Vulnerabilities — Establish and maintain a process to accept and address reports of software vulnerabilities, including providing a means for external entities to report. The process is to include such items as: a vulnerability handling policy that identifies reporting process, responsible party for handling vulnerability reports, and a process for intake, assignment, remediation, and remediation testing. As part of the process, use a vulnerability tracking system that includes severity ratings and metrics for measuring timing for identification, analysis, and remediation of vulnerabilities. Review and update documentation annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard. Third-party application developers need to consider this an externally-facing policy that helps to set expectations for outside stakeholders.
items.rec: Establish a process to accept and address reports of software vulnerabilities, including those affecting internally built applications and automations.

items.q: Perform Root Cause Analysis on Security Vulnerabilities — Perform root cause analysis on security vulnerabilities. When reviewing vulnerabilities, root cause analysis is the task of evaluating underlying issues that create vulnerabilities in code, and allows development teams to move beyond just fixing individual vulnerabilities as they arise.
items.rec: Perform root cause analysis on security vulnerabilities found in internally developed or configured applications, so recurring causes are addressed.

items.q: Establish and Manage an Inventory of Third-Party Software Components — Establish and manage an updated inventory of third-party components used in development, often referred to as a “bill of materials,” as well as components slated for future use. This inventory is to include any risks that each third-party component could pose. Evaluate the list at least monthly to identify any changes or updates to these components, and validate that the component is still supported.
items.rec: Establish an inventory of third-party software components in use, including low-code platform connectors and libraries.

items.q: Use Up-to-Date and Trusted Third-Party Software Components — Use up-to-date and trusted third-party software components. When possible, choose established and proven frameworks and libraries that provide adequate security. Acquire these components from trusted sources or evaluate the software for vulnerabilities before use.
items.rec: Use only up-to-date and trusted third-party software components, with a defined process for reviewing and updating them.

items.q: Establish and Maintain a Severity Rating System and Process for Application Vulnerabilities — Establish and maintain a severity rating system and process for application vulnerabilities that facilitates prioritizing the order in which discovered vulnerabilities are fixed. This process includes setting a minimum level of security acceptability for releasing code or applications. Severity ratings bring a systematic way of triaging vulnerabilities that improves risk management and helps ensure the most severe bugs are fixed first. Review and update the system and process annually.
items.rec: Establish a severity rating system and process for application vulnerabilities, aligned to the wider vulnerability management SLAs.

items.q: Use Standard Hardening Configuration Templates for Application Infrastructure — Use standard, industry-recommended hardening configuration templates for application infrastructure components. This includes underlying servers, databases, and web servers, and applies to cloud containers, Platform as a Service (PaaS) components, and SaaS components. Do not allow in-house developed software to weaken configuration hardening.
items.rec: Use standard hardening configuration templates for application infrastructure, applied consistently to new and existing deployments.

items.q: Separate Production and Non-Production Systems — Maintain separate environments for production and non-production systems.
items.rec: Separate production and non-production environments for all development activity, including low-code applications currently built directly in production.

items.q: Train Developers in Application Security Concepts and Secure Coding — Ensure that all software development personnel receive training in writing secure code for their specific development environment and responsibilities. Training can include general security principles and application security standard practices. Conduct training at least annually and design in a way to promote security within the development team, and build a culture of security among the developers.
items.rec: Provide application security and secure coding training to everyone building applications and automations, including business users developing on low-code platforms.

items.q: Leverage Vetted Modules or Services for Application Security Components — Leverage vetted modules or services for application security components, such as identity management, encryption, auditing, and logging. Using platform features in critical security functions will reduce developers’ workload and minimize the likelihood of design or implementation errors. Modern operating systems provide effective mechanisms for identification, authentication, and authorization and make those mechanisms available to applications. Use only standardized, currently accepted, and extensively reviewed encryption algorithms. Operating systems also provide mechanisms to create and maintain secure audit logs.
items.rec: Use vetted modules or services for application security components such as authentication, encryption and logging, rather than bespoke implementations.

items.q: Implement Code-Level Security Checks — Apply static and dynamic analysis tools within the application life cycle to verify that secure coding practices are being followed.
items.rec: Implement code-level security checks through static and dynamic analysis tooling integrated into the development process.

items.q: Conduct Application Penetration Testing — Conduct application penetration testing. For critical applications, authenticated penetration testing is better suited to finding business logic vulnerabilities than code scanning and automated security testing. Penetration testing relies on the skill of the tester to manually manipulate an application as an authenticated and unauthenticated user.
items.rec: Conduct application penetration testing on externally facing and business-critical applications on a defined cycle.

items.q: Conduct Threat Modeling — Conduct threat modeling. Threat modeling is the process of identifying and addressing application security design flaws within a design, before code is created. It is conducted through specially trained individuals who evaluate the application design and gauge security risks for each entry point and access level. The goal is to map out the application, architecture, and infrastructure in a structured way to understand its weaknesses.
items.rec: Conduct threat modelling for applications handling sensitive data or exposed externally, and use the output to drive control selection.

items.q: Designate Personnel to Manage Incident Handling — Designate one key person, and at least one backup, who will manage the enterprise’s incident handling process. Management personnel are responsible for the coordination and documentation of incident response and recovery efforts and can consist of employees internal to the enterprise, service providers, or a hybrid approach. If using a service provider, designate at least one person internal to the enterprise to oversee any third-party work. Review annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard.
items.rec: Maintain designated incident handling personnel with a named deputy, and provide formal incident response training so the role is supported by capability as well as assignment.

items.q: Establish and Maintain Contact Information for Reporting Security Incidents — Establish and maintain contact information for parties that need to be informed of security incidents. Contacts may include internal staff, service providers, law enforcement, cyber insurance providers, relevant government agencies, Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC) partners, or other stakeholders. Verify contacts annually to ensure that information is up-to-date.
items.rec: Validate the notification process end to end, including regulator contact details and the applicable reporting clocks, and rehearse the notification steps so timelines can be met under pressure. (CSF RS.CO-02: Internal and external stakeholders are notified of incidents)

items.q: Establish and Maintain an Enterprise Process for Reporting Incidents — Establish and maintain a documented enterprise process for the workforce to report security incidents. The process includes reporting timeframe, personnel to report to, mechanism for reporting, and the minimum information to be reported. Ensure the process is publicly available to all of the workforce. Review annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard.
items.rec: Maintain the enterprise incident reporting process with an accessible reporting mechanism, publicised to all staff and reinforced through training.

items.q: Establish and Maintain an Incident Response Process — Establish and maintain a documented incident response process that addresses roles and responsibilities, compliance requirements, and a communication plan. Review annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard.
items.rec: Exercise the incident response plan at least annually, including relevant third parties such as the managed service provider, insurer and legal counsel, and update the plan with the lessons identified. (CSF RS.MA-01: The incident response plan is executed in coordination with relevant t…)

items.q: Assign Key Roles and Responsibilities — Assign key roles and responsibilities for incident response, including staff from legal, IT, information security, facilities, public relations, human resources, incident responders, analysts, and relevant third parties. Review annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard.
items.rec: Assign and keep current the key incident response roles and responsibilities, refreshing named individuals whenever personnel change and rehearsing the assignments.

items.q: Define Mechanisms for Communicating During Incident Response — Determine which primary and secondary mechanisms will be used to communicate and report during a security incident. Mechanisms can include phone calls, emails, secure chat, or notification letters. Keep in mind that certain mechanisms, such as emails, can be affected during a security incident. Review annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard.
items.rec: Prepare approved holding statements and agreed public communication channels in advance, and rehearse external communication as part of the incident exercise. (CSF RC.CO-04: Public updates on incident recovery are shared using approved methods …)

items.q: Conduct Routine Incident Response Exercises — Plan and conduct routine incident response exercises and scenarios for key personnel involved in the incident response process to prepare for responding to real-world incidents. Exercises need to test communication channels, decision making, and workflows. Conduct testing on an annual basis, at a minimum.
items.rec: Conduct routine incident response exercises at least annually, covering both technical response and management decision-making, and feed the findings back into the plan.

items.q: Conduct Post-Incident Reviews — Conduct post-incident reviews. Post-incident reviews help prevent incident recurrence through identifying lessons learned and follow-up action.
items.rec: Perform and document root cause analysis for all incidents meeting the defined severity threshold, and track resulting actions to closure. (CSF RS.AN-03: Analysis is performed to establish what has taken place during an inci…)

items.q: Establish and Maintain Security Incident Thresholds — Establish and maintain security incident thresholds, including, at a minimum, differentiating between an incident and an event. Examples can include: abnormal activity, security vulnerability, security weakness, data breach, privacy incident, etc. Review annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard.
items.rec: Define specific, testable criteria for initiating recovery and require a recorded sign-off before restoration begins. (CSF RS.MA-05: The criteria for initiating incident recovery are applied)

items.q: Establish and Maintain a Penetration Testing Program — Establish and maintain a penetration testing program appropriate to the size, complexity, industry, and maturity of the enterprise. Penetration testing program characteristics include scope, such as network, web application, Application Programming Interface (API), hosted services, and physical premise controls; frequency; limitations, such as acceptable hours, and excluded attack types; point of contact information; remediation, such as how findings will be routed internally; and retrospective requirements.
items.rec: Establish a penetration testing programme with a defined scope, cadence and year-on-year comparison, rather than commissioning tests as isolated purchases.

items.q: Perform Periodic External Penetration Tests — Perform periodic external penetration tests based on program requirements, no less than annually. External penetration testing must include enterprise and environmental reconnaissance to detect exploitable information. Penetration testing requires specialized skills and experience and must be conducted through a qualified party. The testing may be clear box or opaque box.
items.rec: Maintain periodic external penetration testing by a suitably accredited provider on a defined cycle.

items.q: Remediate Penetration Test Findings — Remediate penetration test findings based on the enterprise’s documented vulnerability remediation process. This should include determining a timeline and level of effort based on the impact and prioritization of each identified finding.
items.rec: Remediate penetration test findings within the documented SLA, prioritising the high-severity findings currently past due, and track them in the central remediation register.

items.q: Validate Security Measures — Validate security measures after each penetration test. If deemed necessary, modify rulesets and capabilities to detect the techniques used during testing.
items.rec: Validate that security measures work as intended through control validation exercises such as breach and attack simulation or purple team activity.

items.q: Perform Periodic Internal Penetration Tests — Perform periodic internal penetration tests based on program requirements, no less than annually. The testing may be clear box or opaque box.
items.rec: Perform periodic internal penetration testing to assess exposure from an assumed-breach position on the internal network.

references.note: Cross-references are the official CIS Controls v8.1 to NIST CSF v2.0 mapping (24 June 2024). Each relationship reads from the safeguard to the subcategory: a safeguard marked Subset is narrower than the CSF outcome, Superset is broader, Equivalent covers the same ground.
